title: ISRO's NVS-03 Launch Tonight Aims to Restore NavIC's Standalone Positioning
excerpt: GSLV-F18 is set to lift off at 11:51 p.m. IST on October 30 carrying NVS-03, which would take NavIC to four working navigation satellites — the minimum for standalone positioning — after years of clock failures and the NVS-02 setback.
body:
• ISRO is scheduled to launch the NVS-03 navigation satellite aboard GSLV-F18 at 11:51 p.m. IST on October 30 from Sriharikota.
  • Only three of NavIC's planned seven satellites currently provide navigation services; four are the minimum for standalone positioning, the government told Parliament in July.
  • NVS-02, launched in January 2025, reached its transfer orbit but could not raise its orbit after a disconnected connector starved a pyro valve of its firing signal.
  • NVS-03 carries an indigenous atomic clock and adds the L1 signal alongside L5 and S-band; the real test comes after launch, during orbit-raising.

The Indian Space Research Organisation is set to launch NVS-03, the third satellite in its second-generation navigation series, aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket at 11:51 p.m. IST on Thursday, October 30, from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota. The mission is an attempt to pull NavIC, India's regional satellite navigation system, back above the minimum it needs to fix positions on its own.

A constellation below strength

NavIC — Navigation with Indian Constellation — was designed around seven satellites covering India and a region extending roughly 1,500 kilometres beyond its borders. In a written reply to Parliament on July 29, Space Minister Jitendra Singh disclosed that only three satellites were providing navigation services, while at least four are required for basic positioning. The system, he said, cannot currently offer standalone positioning, although its timing services remain functional. A position fix needs simultaneous signals from at least four satellites; below that number, receivers must lean on other systems such as GPS.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=iRsOsYU1p74

"IST on Thursday, October 30, from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota."

How NavIC got here

The constellation was hollowed out over a decade. Several first-generation IRNSS satellites lost their imported rubidium atomic clocks — without precise timing, a navigation satellite cannot produce usable ranging signals. Then came NVS-02. Launched in January 2025, it reached its transfer orbit and deployed its solar panels, but never completed the engine burns needed to reach its operational slot. An ISRO review published on February 25, 2026 identified a disconnected connector in the drive signal to an oxidiser-line pyro valve as the most likely cause, affecting both the primary and redundant paths. For NVS-03, ISRO has reportedly prepared the satellite with its pyro valves already open before launch, removing the specific failure point — and putting the remaining propulsion controls under sharper scrutiny.

What NVS-03 carries

The roughly 2,250-kilogram satellite will be placed into an elliptical transfer orbit with a perigee of 170 kilometres and an apogee of 37,023 kilometres at an inclination of 20.75 degrees, according to ISRO's mission brochure. NVS-03 carries an indigenous rubidium atomic clock alongside procured clocks — the domestic clock programme is a direct response to the imported-clock failures — and it broadcasts on the L1 band at 1,575.42 MHz in addition to the existing L5 and S-band signals. The L1 signal is the band most widely supported by consumer devices, which matters for handset adoption.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DfGSYc2Bfa8/

What to watch

Lift-off is only the first test. After separation, NVS-03 must fire its own engine in a series of orbit-raising manoeuvres — exactly the phase where NVS-02 was lost — before commissioning can begin. ISRO has not announced when the satellite is expected to enter navigation service. Follow-on satellites NVS-04 and NVS-05 are in development to rebuild the constellation toward its seven-satellite design.
